have pleased Hunt for its assertion of the poet’s native independence of mind. In the poem,
S. returns in a lighter tone and a minor key to the theme of the poet’s relation to ‘wealth or
power’, which he had elaborated at length in PB3 and evoked briefly in the fragment Proteus
Wordsworth, who shall bind thee? (Longman iii 160–1, no. 243). In the Dedication to PB3, S.
says of the poet Peter, a satirical portrait of Wordsworth: ‘He changes colours like a chame-
leon, and his coat like a snake’ (32–3). Traditional emblem of inconstancy and flattery, from
its ability to change the colour of its skin, the chameleon is among the ‘creeping things that
creep upon the earth’ which are considered to be contagiously unclean in Leviticus xi 29–44.
 Text from 1820. The capitalisation of Harvard Nbk 1 has been adopted. Punctuation has been
slightly modified after consulting the draft in Nbk 10, the Harvard Nbk 1 fair copy, and 1839.
